['Mr. Speaker, one of the most important issues facing Canada today, particularly the Atlantic region, is passenger transportation. The royal commission which is now underway will have a great bearing on the future for travel within our great country.
Because transportation pressures are mounting in all directions, it becomes essential for the commission to work with a sense of urgency and to make its recommendations as early as possible. In the meanwhile, it is also essential that we hold a steady course with present services.
For example, in Atlantic Canada we reluctantly accepted the need for reduction in VIA Rail services to match budgets and levels of service. We endure a Trans-Canada Highway that is inadequate and dangerous until we are able to find ways to improve upon it. One saving grace for Atlantic transportation, however, has been the improvement in air services in recent years. But even these are now challenged by proposals for increased landing fees and other charges to enhance transport cost recovery.
Surely, these new charges can be deferred until the royal commission report is complete in a comprehensive context. We must not any longer approach passenger transportation one segment at a time. The future demands a total solution.']

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the criticism of the Israeli police by the recent commission of inquiry into the tragic events in Old Jerusalem.
Israeli security forces should not have trusted Islamic religious authorities who were notified that a fringe Jewish group would not be allowed to enter Temple Mount. Muslims proceeded to defile this holy site with an illegal, planned attack on Jewish worshippers. Rioters were incited over loudspeakers to slaughter the Jews.
Israeli police showed great restraint in not using live ammunition against the stone throwers as they attacked police and then thousands of praying Jews at the Western Wall. The police officers who had been forced to retreat re-entered the Temple Mount to rescue officers and to prevent the thousands of rioters from seizing weapons and ammunition in the police station. Only then did they use live ammunition in life threatening situations.
When will Palestinians and Muslim extremists learn that Israelis will never agree to their self-determination if they cannot be trusted to respect the basic human rights of others? When will the world learn that sanctioning attacks on innocent victims leads to further violence, not peace?

Mr. Speaker, Transport Canada's decision to implement a cost-recovery program for air services in April, 1991 can only hurt airports and air services in Atlantic Canada and further alienate Atlantic Canadians.
Higher fees on airport operations will raise air service costs beyond the point which is affordable by the vast majority of Atlantic Canadians, or even shut down smaller operations altogether.
The government again has abandoned Atlantic Canada with its virtual withdrawal of passenger rail services from the region, the steadily deteriorating condition of the Trans-Canada Highway, and the rising costs for users of Marine Atlantic ferries, ports, and harbours.
Prince Edward Island spends more per capita on transportation than any other province. We spend 4 per cent of our gross domestic product on this sector, while having the lowest GDP in Canada. Higher air service costs could cripple an already vulnerable transportation system in P.E.I. and in the rest of Atlantic Canada.

Mr. Speaker, when the labour dispute between the United Steelworkers of America and Stelco and Algoma Steel Corporation does finally come to an end, and if we are to believe the assertions of the corporations and the predictions of steel analysts, fewer than 80 per cent of the steelworkers will be called back to work. This figure has been used as a precedence based on an arbitrary figure which signals the end of a labour dispute, the workers eligible for UI benefits after that.
We ask the minister to utilize the flexibility given her to reduce the 80 per cent figure to 30, 40 or whatever

percentage is appropriate so those people who have been without any money for 12 weeks and counting will become eligible without any long bureaucratic delay. We ask the minister to demonstrate compassion and exercise authority to reassure these 16,000 steelworkers that indeed they will immediately be eligible for benefits if not recalled to work.

Mr. Speaker, in little over a month, the NHL board of governors will be granting new hockey franchises to the league. Two Canadian applications are up for consideration: Hamilton and our own capital, Ottawa.
Given the spirit of fair competition it appears obvious to me that we in Canada should be first in line for a team. We have the money, the talent, the heritage, and the know-how. Hockey is our home game.
As our present Governor General said in the Chamber in 1983, "The National Hockey League is a type of public trust. More than that, hockey is central to the Canadian identity."
In addition, hockey has become big business on the international stage. We must not allow a group of backroom boys to dilute our leadership in this game by granting franchises to interests whose only familiarity with ice is in their whisky.
I call upon all members of Parliament to rally their constituents by circulating a petition in support of the two Canadian bids. Copies are available in my office.
And, finally, to the NHL board of directors I say: when Canada plays hockey, hockey wins.

Mr. Speaker, last week the United Nations celebrated its 45th year of dedication to world peace and international good order. It is with gratitude that we note that the United Nations has probably never been closer to achieving its original mandate than during the last few months of the Gulf crisis.
However, despite the UN solidarity on the Middle East to date, there is growing concern that the agenda being followed by Canada and others is that of the United States, not the UN. One questions whether or
not the U.S. is using the UN for its own, and not the international, good. Have we been led to UN commitments which entrap us into following from here on a U.S. agenda?
The UN is currently owed $600 million in late support payments from 17 countries world-wide. Of this, $482 million is back debt owed from the United States. Actions speak louder than words. What is the U.S. commitment to the UN? The government must insist that the U.S. prove its commitment to the UN and what it stands for by paying its debt to the UN.

subtopic: THE LEADER OF THE LIBERAL PARTY
THE LEADER OF THE LIBERAL PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many of my constituents agree with the Prime Minister, who says Jean Chretien is a man who keeps changing his mind. Mr. Speaker, I think they are right.
I\vo days ago, Mr. Chretien announced he would scrap the GST if his party formed the next government. A few weeks ago, however, Mr. Chretien admitted it would be irresponsible to get rid of the GST without proposing a new tax formula. It didn't take long for him to change his mind.
On the constitutional issue, a few months ago Jean Chretien favoured a strong central government. Today, he talks about changing the powers given to the provinces.

Mr. Speaker, Jean Chretien keeps changing his mind, fails to provide leadership and has no vision for the future of this country.

Mr. Speaker, there is presently in Ontario alone a backlog of 44,220 English-speaking refugees waiting to be processed.
The Auditor General's report states: "The system was extremely prone to large-scale abuses and became overloaded by a growing number of claims that compounded existing delays." It continues: "Changes had either not been implemented or were not operating as intended."
We have reached this point. The Toronto office alone is facing 22,000 cases. It will be able to handle only 7,000 cases within the next year. In an attempt to deal with this, present policy dictates that only English-speaking refugee cases be processed.
The Auditor General clearly states: "The backlog clearance program will cost more than estimated."
Clearly, this is a complete failure. I ask the minister when will she act responsibly and announce immediate measures to solve this inhumane and unacceptable situation.

Mr. Speaker, recently, I attended a press conference to draw the attention of the public to the important work being done in my riding. I am referring to the development strategy submitted by the Laurentides community development assistance board.
This tool will have a positive impact on the entire region. The development strategy will help members of our community make wise choices and concentrate on priority projects. The strategy is the result of effective regional consultation, reflecting the enthusiasm and energy of our community.
The Laurentides community development assistance board is to be commended for a job well done, and I urge residents to take part in these consultation exercises so that we can achieve balanced development in our community.

They are: Wellwood of Canada, with a profit of $110 million in 1989 and a $2.8 million tax credit, and no taxes paid.
Shame.

Shame.

Shame.

The winner is: CP Hotels. This corporation did not pay any taxes in 1989 and still received over $2 million in government hand-outs.
Congratulations to all our contestants for showing us how to avoid paying taxes by using the loopholes that are already in existence.
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance.
Today, Statistics Canada, the government's own statistical agency, stated: "Economic growth turned clearly
October 31, 1990

negative in August." Gross domestic product, the overall size of the economy actually fell 0.5 per cent, the largest monthly drop in almost five years. Under the government's policies, the economy actually shrank in August.
These cold numbers do not begin to tell the full story of the pain, the suffering, and the damage caused by the government's policies for hundreds of thousands of workers, farmers, and small business people.
Will the minister, today, change his policies and bring in new policies that will not cause this economy to shrink? Instead, will he bring in policies that will cause economic growth and that will not destroy jobs but will create them for people all across the country?

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the comments of the Leader of the Opposition and he is quite right. The size of the economy declined by half of 1 per cent in the month of August.
I want to point out to him, so that people do not get the wrong impression from the exaggeration of his words, the economy grew in both July and June.
I have made it quite clear since the Budget of this year that the government was expecting some decline in the economy. I also have said that after seven and a half years of very strong growth, growth which started to exceed our capacity as a country and as a economy to handle, that there were bound to be some inflationary pressures and also some decline in the economy because economies cannot grow forever. That is the sort of period that we are going through.
It is an unfortunate thing that this is the sort of thing that does happen in an economy. We have to work our way through it. Interest rates have been coming down during the month of August. Every week the interest rates declined. That is the response that we have made in order to get the economy back on a sound footing so we can see a period of solid growth ahead.

Mr. Speaker, this morning at 8 a.m. in Sydney, Nova Scotia, the owner of three gigantic factory ships from St. Malo,
France, boarded one of these vessels, having brought along the press from Paris to witness his stated threat that he will ram any vessel from any country that tries to stop him from illegally fishing in so-called Canada-France disputed waters. They fished there all day Friday and they fished for the last three nights in Canadian waters with no observer aboard.
I want to ask the Minister of Fisheries now, why is this government unwilling to protect a signed quota agreement between Canada and France? Why is it that the only party trying to stop them tonight is a tiny military vessel from St. Pierre?
Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and
Oceans): Mr. Speaker, the fishermen in Newfoundland and Labrador are going to be impressed. Today, we have the Newfoundland member defending the interests of the fishermen of St. Pierre and Miquelon. I guess the member is right.
There is a problem between la flotte metropolitaine frangaise and les pecheurs de Saint-Pierre et Miquelon. Surely, the member is not advocating that we intervene in a French matter and tell France how to treat its fishermen in St. Pierre and Miquelon, because that is a problem.

Mr. Speaker, the minister would have us believe that for the last three nights they have not been fishing while they have been in the Canadian zone 80 miles off our coast with no observer aboard.
What does he think they have been doing, having a Tupperware party?
How can this minister expect-when his main duty is to protect the fishing resource for Canadians-Canadians to believe that three massive factory freezer trawlers fishing an already depleted resource which we claim is ours is none of Canada's business?

Is this government now telling France: "Here's the fish, the zone is yours"?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Much has been said lately about the preparations for war in the Persian Gulf. The U.S. president has been planning military action with the congressional leaders.
Saddam Hussein has said that Iraq is preparing for a war and expects a U.S. attack. Last week, the external affairs minister said that Canadian young men and women may not come home for Christmas, or at all, and began to talk about Canada's participation in a war.
My question to the Prime Minister is this. The government has done a lot to prepare for war. What has his government done, using our seat on the UN Security Council, to prevent a war? Specifically, what has the Prime Minister and his government done?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure if the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party reads The New York Times. If she does, she will know that about four or five weeks ago when there was a very serious dispute within the United Nations, within the Security Council as to whether auspices of the United Nations would be used or not, it was the leading intervention of Canada that helped encourage all members of the Security Council to operate within United Nations auspices.
She will know, if she is interested, that the Government of Canada, through our ambassador to the United Nations, has been highly instrumental in achieving the
Oral Questions
consensus that we have found so far on the resolutions that have come with both unanimity and impact upon Saddam Hussein from the Security Council. We have in addition been in touch at all levels of the government, calls made by the Prime Minister directly on the telephone, conversations the Prime Minister and I both had during the Children's Summit at the United Nations with foreign leaders, contacts by a range of our ambassadors and representatives seeking ways in which we can first make clear to Saddam Hussein that the world wants him out of Kuwait and that that is a condition precedent to other changes that might occur.
Canada has a very important diplomatic card to play. We are playing it very effectively. We intend to continue to play it as effectively as we can. If the hon. member wants, as her status as a party leader would entitle her to, a more detailed briefing so that she could speak from the facts, I would be delighted to provide that.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the minister responsible for external affairs.
The facts are that Canada has escalated the talk of a war, has not escalated the talk of peace at all, and to tell Canadians last week that their sons and daughters might never even come home from the Middle East is not advocating for peace.
Hear, hear.

The minister for external affairs, Mr. Speaker, talks about UN resolutions. This government chose, without reference to the Canadian Parliament, to send ships to enforce an economic blockade in the Middle East. Presumably the government did this thinking that an economic blockade would be successful. No one agrees with Saddam Hussein's actions.
I ask the minister responsible for External Affairs, when this was done how long did the government plan to give the economic blockade in order to see if it was going to be effective? It seems that only last week the economic blockade was seen to be effective, the next day the minister for external affairs was telling Canadians their sons and daughters might not return home.

Hear, hear.

October 31, 1990

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:

We regret the fact and wish we could rewrite history about the way children in residential schools were subjected apparently to physical and sexual harassment many years ago.

the government's response to these terrible problems. I will table that letter if it be the wish of the House.

This has resulted in the undermining of communications between native people, and between native and non-native Canadians. This cut in funding has also further jeopardized the survival of aboriginal languages in Canada and compromised the efforts to improve native literacy.
The petitioners pray that the government should reinstate both the native communications programs and the Northern Broadcast Access Program at full funding levels and, further, that the Department of the Secretary of State conduct consultations with the groups affected before it changes the funding plans for native communications media.

Mr. Speaker, I will look with a great deal of interest at the amendment placed before us by the government, as I have just seen it this morning.
In the meantime, I would like to generally address this bill. The section that is being discussed now is in Part I and it is the definition section of the bill. I would suggest that it is a reflection of the problems with this bill. It is the key reason why this bill is flawed and unacceptable.
Unfortunately, although desperately needed in many of the new changes that have been made-and I think the committee under its several chairman did an outstanding job as well as the legislative committee-the government put in definitions that make it like building your Canadian house on the San Andreas fault. It is on a faulty foundation. It has been built with the potential to crack and split so that the balkanization of this country occurs rather than using this very powerful communication tool, this wonderful potential of infrastructure, or as the Prime Minister called it, "the central nervous system of our society", which will promote and communicate cultural values to our young generation, in particular. It will be maintained under federal jurisdiction to ensure that we have a common interest in common policies and

October 31, 1990
Government Orders
a common modality of operation from coast to coast on all three sides.
That is not the case. Bill C-40 attempts to redefine broadcasting, thereby touching provincial jurisdiction in the way that it has been done. This could result in a provincial challenge to this jurisdiction. The problem is further compounded by a move to separate cable services-it is referred to as the undertakings-into programming and non-programming functions. This is a rejection, as the government well knows, of conventional legal practice which regards such undertakings as indivisible.
This principle lies at the veiy heart of the CRTC's ability to regulate broadcasting to balance services, costs, benefits and to ensure that Canadians have reasonable access and choice, regardless of whether they are looking at alpha numeric text, whether they are seeing stationary or moving objects, whether they are going to be entertained or informed or whatever the case may be.
This government knows very well that some years ago the Government of Quebec indicated its interest in regulating communications beginning with cable television. Recently, with the destabilizing factors that are going on in our society, and the questions that flowed from Meech Lake and everything else, we had some very serious concerns. Then there was the provincial minister of communications of Quebec expressing serious reservations about this being maintained in the federal jurisdiction. In her view, and she spoke quite candidly and openly, broadcasting and communication functions are culturally relative. It was her view, and I presume she was expressing the view of the Government of Quebec, that this was an exclusive jurisdiction belonging to the province of Quebec.
Constitutional experts have already pointed out that the challenges to federal jurisdiction in areas like broadcasting will now become inevitable because Bill C-40 seems designed to weaken any possible defence and indeed, to set the stage, for a devolution of authority and indeed the balkanization of service which would inevitably follow.
I suggest that this is sad. We are all very much aware that, as a general rule of statutory interpretation, when a term is changed in law, a new meaning could be ascribed to the changed term. This is very disconcerting.
We struggled long to ensure a balance of broadcasting services and programming choices across this immense land of ours. It is an equity that is still not fully balanced in terms of interests and resources, but we are getting there. We are getting very good.
Only if one would contemplate circumstances in which neither Canadian ownership nor Canadian programming is any longer relevant or important does this kind of voluntary abdication of the federal role make any kind of sense at all.
Regarding what I was referring to with respect to the splitting of the undertaking or the splitting up of the cable services, this proposed act would create a constitutional issue and give rise to dual regulation by splitting this whole undertaking into two parts: programming and non-programming.
I am going to quote from the CRTC, the regulator, which is a quasi-judicial court which came before the legislative committee. In fact, it has come before us on two occasions and said to us: "Be very cautious. Be very careful. You have changed the rules of the game. You have now taken the non-programming part out of the system."
This very arbitrary split is serious, and I would like to explain why. The Supreme Court of Canada has held that for constitutional purposes, broadcasting undertakings are not divisible into their component parts. That is what the Supreme Court said, the rationale being that as far as possible, no single undertaking should be subject to two separate masters or jurisdictions.
This government was well aware of that. In fact, it made provisions further on in the bill in clause 85, or 87 since we have changed the numbers, that it would now fall under other provisions.
The proposed legislation would require such a split and therefore would reopen the debate over constitutional jurisdiction, especially with regard to cable distribution systems.
October 31, 1990

The proposed act implicitly states that it does not agree with the 1932 Privy Council radio reference case which assigned federal jurisdiction through two arguments: that of peace, order and good government as well as that of radio waves which are interprovincial and international. They have suggested that this is wrong.
Second, the proposed act implicitly states again that the Supreme Court of Canada was wrong when it concluded that undertakings could not or should not be split. As the Supreme Court did decide in both the Dionne and the Capital Cities cases. It also said that with respect to the AGT, the Alberta Government Telephone case.
Legislation now invites provinces and others to start new litigation, but with federal jurisdiction on much weaker ground because the legislation itself admits that a split is a practicable alternative. I find that sad.
One example, typical of the problems associated with the splitting of undertakings, is the following. Engineering experts have advised us that the intellectual matter contained in the vertical blanking intervals of a television signal can be considered to be separate and apart from the main transmission. That is all gobbledegook to many of us.
What it literally means is that the broadcasters use this blanking interval to distribute closed captioned, alpha numeric material for the hearing impaired. The definition of "program" will therefore mean that the commission will lose its jurisdiction over this very important aspect of broadcasting.
It is rather ludicrous, because we just finished bringing the whole question of hearing impaired into the bill. So now we put it in. We take it out. We play games with it without even thinking of the consequences. It is really a sad state.
It should also be remembered that if alpha numeric material is not regulated, then alpha numeric networks could be freely set up and such operations could be owned by foreign interests. I sincerely invite the parliamentary secretary and, through him, the minister to rethink the serious implications of what they have done in their definition section. Without maintaining the jurisdiction of the commission as it is under the present broadcasting act, they have put this whole system in
Government Orders
jeopardy and nonprogramming activities of cable licensees could fall outside the jurisdiction of this law.
I suggest that one regulator with jurisdiction over the entire undertaking would be able to ensure that programming has its primary place in the system. The CRTC could examine and then decide to exempt under clause 9.4 of the bill, and that would look after the concerns that we have if we return to the original definition.
Mr. Speaker, what is this TV set? I ask you that. What does the TV set in your home do? It informs you, it entertains you, it enlightens you, it gives you the weather, it gives you the stock market, the news, laughs through comedy, tears through drama, it educates you and your children. The minute you turn on your set it impacts on your life. It has a very special kind of place. You can even be a couch potato and enjoy it.
It is also a business, but it is a very special business that must be so treated whether it is home-shopping services, whether it is your favourite TV or movie, whether it is your favourite program such as Lance et Compte, E.N.G., Street Legal, Le Point, that is not the issue.
The government's attempt to produce a technology-neutral bill that is supposed to survive the time and introduction of new technologies is going to result in serious concerns and litigation. I would like to recommend strongly that we go back to the original definition so that we do not need to worry that this well-designed Canadian broadcasting system which can establish the unique cultural identity of our country in any man's language is ever put into jeopardy.
Therefore, I would move that Liberal Motions Nos. 1, 2, 3, and 4 be reinserted in the definitions found in the 1968 Broadcasting Act. They have stood the test of time. I would suggest that in terms of Canadian content and the potential to siphon out much-needed advertising revenue dollars which are needed for Canadian programs can be more carefully reviewed by the CRTC. I remind this government that this is not the act for the sale of Canada. This is an act for the Canadian broadcasting system which impacts on the lives of our children and determines our future and who we are as a people.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this bill as a former NDP communications critic, moved on into the justice area,

Government Orders
but I have with me my friend from Okanagan-Shuswap who-
Are you still NDP?

Yes, I am still NDP and proud of it, my friend. Proud of it.
My colleague from Okanagan-Shuswap, who is now the critic, will be working with me on this bill. This bill has been before us for a long time. It is a very complicated bill.
What we are going to tiy to do from the NDP perspective is to try to make it comprehensible to the average person who may be watching this debate, reading about it, or sitting here following it. We undertake to try and do that to the best of our ability.
The bill, as the previous Liberal member mentioned, is of immense importance. We do watch TV for news, entertainment, education, information, and soon we are going to be watching it and using it to order our pizzas, to do our banking, order our groceries. Indeed, we will even be able to replay our favourite hockey game, the hockey goal. When my Vancouver Canucks beat your team there in Edmonton, Mr. Speaker, occasionally, we will be able to replay the plays even in our own house. We see that kind of new technology that is always coming in.
There is immense power and immense money involved in communications and that is why this bill is of immense importance.
I want to outline a little bit, before getting to the first stage of amendment, the history of the bill. It has been a very long road indeed.
In May 1985 the minister, who was also the minister then, created a task force on broadcasting, which became known as the Caplan-Sauvageau report. The task force reported in September 1986. In May 1988 the 15th standing committee report was a major report on broadcasting. In June 1988 the then Minister of Communications, Flora MacDonald tabled Bill C-136, which was the Broadcast Act. She also tabled Canadian Voices, Canadian Choices, a broadcasting policy document.
From July to August 1988, hearings were held on Bill C-136. We had 15 meetings, heard numerous witnesses and considered dozens of amendments. I am pleased to say that the government accepted six NDP amendments
and two Liberal amendments, which is kind of unusual, but the way committees should work.
Our party's amendments were successful on matters dealing with multiculturalism, regional representations, equal rights for women and other groups, and other issues. In September 1988 we had six days of debate on the report stage. There were 92 opposition amendments and while some minor amendments were accepted, the government rejected the major amendments on the bill.
The bill passed third reading on September 28, 1988-that is about two years ago-and the bill died in the Senate three days later when the Prime Minister called an election which, unfortunately, he won.
In October 1989 the bill was back. This time it was called Bill C-40. It is essentially the same bill with five or six changes. I know the parliamentary secretary, my good friend, the member from Edmonton, has done a yeoman's job on this bill, and before that, in committee. The government should take notice of this fellow from Alberta. He is not in my party, but he has done a very good job in this House, and in committee beforehand.
Hear, hear.

This bill passed second reading in December 1989. From January to March it was in a legislative committee. There were 65 amendments presented by my colleague for Mount Royal, the Liberal critic, and myself. Most were rejected, although I did manage to get the support of government backbenchers to pass a community broadcasting amendment over the government's objection. It was a great victory for me. Such things do backbenchers live for in this House. It was passed.
The major issues in the debate that we have been presenting are four. First, this government is Meeching and leaching the CBC. Leaching it by taking all the money away and not giving it enough money. "Meeching" it by taking away its ability to have a national mandate for national unity and by splitting the board into English and French. There used to be one board, now it is splitting it up. I call that "Meeching" the bill. There will be much debate about this later on.
Second, the cable industry is the big winner. I feel a little bit like the David against the Goliath of the cable industry here, but David is making a little progress. We want the cable industry regulated, like the phone compa-

ny, so that people will pay decent cable bills. They keep going up and up and up.
Today I presented a petition with about 1,800 signatures. My colleague for Okanagan-Shuswap and I have had petitions from all over this country saying, "Let's regulate the cable industry, like we regulate the TV industry", but unfortunately this bill makes it pretty easy for the cable industry, and it gets off. They can even originate programming, so they are the big winners in this bill.
I have some amendments to level the playing field a little bit. That is what appeals to Conservatives, levelling the playing field, and that is what we are trying to do by some of these amendments.
Third, private television has not been doing its job in presenting Canadian programming, so we have some amendments to make them do that job, since they have the rights to the airwaves.
Fourth, the government is threatening, in our view, the independence of the CRTC, which is the body that regulates radio and television. In making this point, we have some reason to be critical of the commission, but we are going to advocate specific remedies to deal with this. Those will be our amendments.
Now let me just speak briefly to the member for Mount Royal's first group of amendments. I also have some in that group. Basically, by bringing forward Motion No. 3, the hon. member is attempting to delete the exemption from the definition of program for visual images made up largely of alpha numeric text. This is a dangerous exemption, and we support its deletion through this amendment.
Let me try to explain what that means. The government is attempting, by its new definition, to get the CRTC out of the business of regulating services, such as real estate advertising. You see that now on your TV. This potentially exempts such undertakings from Canadian content and ownership provisions. Everything that appears on television, we believe, should have reason to be there, and should either be licensed or not by regulatory authority. There is the potential conflict between regulated channels and non-regulated, or alpha numeric channels, for positions on the television dial.
Government Orders
Let me translate that into English. It means that on the TV dial there is CTV, CBC, but also real estate asking people to buy this and that. What the government does not want to do is regulate that real estate or shopping, or whatever. We think it should be regulated by the CRTC because everything on the dial should be regulated. It should be regulated because that ensures Canadian content. It ensure good taste. It ensures good quality of broadcasting. That is what this amendment is about. That is why we support the amendment of the hon. member for Mount Royal, which is the same amendment we have produced.
I will now sit down, having outlined the nature of our position on the bill. I do not know if I have to move a motion on my amendments in the first grouping, but if I do, I will.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to revisit these issues. As the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam has indicated, we have been here before, and this time maybe we will get it done.
There was a distinguished Canadian broadcaster, who at one point in some discussions leading to the formation of broadcasting policy by the former minister, the Hon. Flora MacDonald, said to the minister, "Here's my advice, Minister. What I believe you ought to do is to repass the old bill and put a clause at the end saying 'this time we mean it'." There was a lot of pith in that comment.
I want to congratulate the hon. member for Mount Royal and the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam for the contributions they made to this bill, the policy we have now and to where we are going. There are other members here in the House who have made like contributions, but I think even the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam will forgive me for a special mention of the hon. member Mount Royal, who has been at this at least as long as I have, and has truly come to these issues with passion, with commitment and with a growing depth of understanding of these issues.
Motions numbered 1, 3, 4, and 5 propose to amend three terms defined in the bill's interpretation clause with respect to the broadcasting, program and radio waves and to remove a subclause clarifying the meaning to be given to other means of telecommunication as it appears in the definition of broadcasting. These defini-

October 31, 1990
Government Orders
tions are crucial to the bill since they serve to define the scope and range of activities which it governs.
First, it is important to know that the definitions are interrelated in that the definition of broadcasting is limited by its inclusion of the terms program and radio waves. This limitation is as intended.
Technological developments have broadened the range and types of information services that can be delivered to the home over telephone wires, by cable and fibre to television screens. Many of these services cannot properly be called broadcasting, and those services should not be regulated under this bill. This legislation is not about information services, which are different in nature from broadcasting. The law must be clear on that point.
On the one hand, this bill is about television programs and radio programs. We want to assure that these activities are regulated because they are cultural in nature and they provide a public service essential to the maintenance and enhancement of national identity and cultural sovereignty.
On the other hand, there is quickly emerging a whole range of new information based services: interactive services, data base services and so on. These are mostly business services, weather services, shopping and real estate services, home security services and the like. These types of activities are not now regulated. The vast majority of these new services are not of a high cultural impact. The mere fact that they may be offered by way of a technology, which until recently has been used primarily for broadcasting, does not in our view constitute grounds for regulation.
The Broadcasting Act should not become an instrument for inhibiting the evolution of new information based services. It is for this reason that the bill has been devised in a technology neutral fashion, focusing on the activities to be regulated, rather than on the technology used for distribution.
That being said, it is important to note that the bill protects the integrity of the broadcasting system in two fundamental ways. First of all, distribution undertakings, such as cable companies, are required to give priority to the carriage of Canadian programming services and in particular to the carriage of local Canadian stations. Second, the CRTC is given express authority to require
distribution undertakings to give priority to the carriage of broadcasting.
It has been claimed that the new definitions could give rise to jurisdictional battles over the regulation of broadcasting undertakings. Yet time and time again the courts have confirmed federal jurisdiction over broadcasting, and recently the Supreme Court confirmed federal jurisdiction over telecommunications. This bill does not jeopardize jurisdiction in any way.
This bill gives the CRTC clear guidelines about which activities are to be regulated as broadcasting. It also gives the commission the latitude it needs to determine how best to regulate undertakings which eventually become involved in both types of activities.
We cannot cling to outdated technological limitations as a basis for regulating a changing environment. The technologies used for broadcasting and telecommunications are converging and this trend appears to be inevitable.
We believe that it is entirely appropriate for legislation to state clearly how each of these distinct activities is to be regulated. We also believe that it is appropriate to have the same regulator govern both activities. The combined effect of amendments Nos. 1, 3, 4 and 5 would be to leave unchanged the wide definitions in the 1968 Broadcasting Act. That would sweep into the scope of the new act many new services which were not foreseen in 1968 and for which there is little or no basis for regulation, broadcasting style.
In the face of technological growth, this approach takes the attitude, "When in doubt regulate". We believe that such an approach is not in the best interest of Canadians.
In our view the new definitions in Bill C-40 provide a more credible and solid basis for the regulation of broadcasting, while at the same time encouraging the evolution of new and exciting information services and the economic development that they entail.
With regard to Motion No. 2, this is a technical amendment and it was brought to the government's attention during the committee study of this bill, that the new definition of the term "network" could be improved to ensure that it covers any arrangement where control over all or any part of the program schedule is delegated to another body. It was pointed out that the existing wording refers only to situations where this control is delegated to another undertaking. In fact, however, this

control can be delegated to a body not licensed as a broadcasting undertaking.
Upon further reflection the government concurred that amending the definition to include delegations of this type would more accurately reflect the realities of today's often complex corporate structures in the broadcasting system and accordingly, the government proposes that this amendment be made.
Finally, with regard to Motion No. 48, this motion proposes amendment of a clause which itself amends another piece of legislation. I am sure you are still with me, Mr. Speaker, the Radiocommunication Act. The purpose of the clause in general is to ensure that the new definitions in the broadcasting legislation line up with those in the Radiocommunication Act, since many enterprises must operate under both.
The Radiocommunication Act governs use of the airways for all kinds of purposes, including broadcasting and broadcasters are required to comply with technical standards established under this legislation before they can obtain a broadcasting licence under the Broadcasting Act. A number of changes were made to the Radiocommunication Act amendments at the committee stage. In the process of inserting these changes, the definition of radio wave, which does appear in the broadcasting definitions, was inadvertently repeated in this clause. This definition is not required here since the term "radio waves" is not used in the Radiocommunication Act. The effect of Motion No. 48 is to remove it.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to pay tribute to the parliamentary secretary, who I think has done a yeoman's job, as have my colleague from Montreal and the gentleman from the New Democratic Party. I think all of them have worked very hard. If we have disagreements, which we do, it has nothing to do with personality.
I think the parliamentary secretary would like to leave us with the notion that all of this is very technical stuff. We are into a new broadcasting age, a new communication age, a new telecommunication age when all we are
Government Orders
doing is changing definitions and updating the legislation which is all very technical stuff.
However, there is much more to it. Politics is involved. Let me explain. In The Globe and Mail just yesterday this government was described, and I usually do not subscribe to this particular columnist's opinion, but this columnist said that this was the most right wing government since R. B. Bennett. You would remember R. B. Bennett, wouldn't you, Mr. Speaker? Even I do. It was the most right wing government in the country.
When this government came to power six years ago it should have put out a shingle saying, "We are going to tear down the institutions of this country. We are going to put holes into the fabric of this country. Whatever was built up the last 40, 50 or 60 years, we are going to tear it down." We have seen it in spades all over.
It is found in this broadcast bill. The government is going to take the mandate of national unity away from the CBC. It is going to split the CBC board into two component parts, one for English and one for French. It is going to break the CRTC up into panels and make these panels into regional monsters. It is going to be wonderful for national unity. It is going to be great for governing this country.
It is already difficult to govern this country. This government is going to make it even worse. In fact, in a way, it has given up on governing the country. It would rather just give it to the market system and turn it over to the capitalists, or give it over to the multinationals, they can run the country better. If people believe that, I have swampland in Florida and I have fairy tales that will make one sleep at night for hours and hours.
Let us define broadcasting. What is the new Broadcasting Act going to do? It is going to balkanize the jurisdiction and services. It is going to split cable services with non-programming on one side and programming on the other. As my esteemed colleague from Montreal says, "What if you get this kind of split in cable services?" One is going to have home shopping on one side, along with real estate services and home security- that will all be very rich and profitable-then siphon off money from the other side, which will be programming.

October 31, 1990
Government Orders
Right? Is that the kind of situation that we want? I do not think so. We are going to balkanize the service and balkanize the jurisdiction.
The CRTC has, over the last number of years, developed a fairly good reputation as a strong national institution. Do we want to harm that institution? Do we want to weaken that institution? I do not think so.
I would like to interject with this. My hon. colleague from Montreal asked for some very germane information pertaining to this piece of legislation.
In fact, my esteemed colleague from Montreal asked for the legal opinions from the department. Mr. Speaker, you would not think that would be very difficult. You would think we would all want to be a little bit more enlightened. We never got them. We are still waiting.
Not only that, but my esteemed colleague from Montreal also filed an access to information request. Guess what? We are still waiting. The question is: What is the hon. parliamentary secretary hiding? What is the hon. Minister of Communications hiding? What is the government hiding? God only knows. When it comes to asking for some, what we would consider to be, legitimate information, the government is not forthcoming.
I think it is absolutely important. It is paramount in the country, particularly at this time, that we keep our national institutions strong and viable. If we do not, the country is going to be in a lot more trouble than it is right now. There are forces at work in the country, right now, right in the House. They would love to undermine the country. They would like to break the underpinnings of this nation. We find them all over the country and in almost every nook and cranny of every institution. We cannot succumb to that, because if we do, the country has not got long to last.
We spent a long time, over 100 years, building up a great country and strong institutions that bind the nation together. It is a huge country and sparsely populated. We need these ties and bonds to keep the country together and to help it grow in unity.
We do not see in this piece of legislation that that is being pursued. The strong central institutions that the country requires are not reflected in this piece of legislation. We do not see it in the new definition of broadcasting. We do not see it in the national unity mandate for the CBC. That mandate would be taken
away. We do not see it in the splitting of CBC board of directors. We do not see it in Balkanizing the CRTC.
We think the government has made a serious mistake, a mis-step, if you wish. It is consistent with its ideology, but it is a serious mistake. We would submit that it go back to the original definition. It has served us well. There is no need to fiddle with this. It is risky. It is dangerous, and it will serve no good.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to address the bill at this stage.
It is quite a comprehensive document. As the newly appointed critic for communications, arts and culture, I have had to bum the midnight oil to come up to speed on a lot of this, which amounts to a very technical and technological bill, to say the least.
My colleagues and I in the New Democratic caucus are certainly relieved to have this bill finally come back before the House. As my colleague, the member for Port Moody-Coquitlam, was pointing out earlier, this bill has been a long time coming. We have seen it at least partially presented in the last Parliament when it went through three readings in this House and finally to the Senate. Essentially, it died on the Order Paper in the Senate at that time.
Now, the bill in somewhat amended form was brought back to this House last November for initial debate and was stalled at that time because of the government's preoccupation with the whole Meech Lake fiasco. All of us in the New Democratic caucus feel very strongly that the country needs a revised and comprehensive Broadcasting Act.
The current act takes us way back to 1968 and much has happened, as we all know, since that time. We have been inundated with technological change and a technological revolution that has been taking place in the country over 10 or 12 years. We have seen the introduction and the very rapid growth of a cable industry that was almost unheard of at that time. There is a real need for a serious look at the legislation and a serious attempt to update and modernize the legislation in terms of today's technology.
The legislation we have before us, although it has some glitches and wrinkles we hope these amendments will be able to smooth out, is very, very critical for Canada, because broadcasting touches all of our lives. It does not matter what age we are at or where we are at in the country, broadcasting touches all of us just about every day. It is an extremely important tool for building a

consensus of identity in the country and for building a consensus for national unity in the country and, believe me, we certainly need a consensus on national unity at this point.
Broadcasting to the 1990s is really what railways were to Canada in the 1800s. It is a mechanism which binds the country together. It ties us together and it builds a family relationship from the east coast to the west coast. Broadcasting is essentially crucial to our democratic process.
Over half of Canadians say that broadcasting is their principal source of news and information, and over 95 per cent of Canadians are radio listeners. That is why, I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, this legislation is so critical and that is why we have taken very, very seriously, as opposition critics, our challenge to make sure that the legislation before the House at the moment is fine-tuned and honed, so that it can do the best job possible in light of technological changes today.
We are presenting 12 or so amendments at this stage, and there are a number of others which will be debated also. But these amendments can be grouped into four main themes or objectives in terms of what we see needs to be beefed up in the current legislation.
First, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, as my colleague pointed out earlier, is being both Meeched and leached. It is being leached in that it is being drained of the life blood needed for the corporation to do the kind of job that it is mandated to do. It needs the kind of funding that is not available through the current legislation. It is being Meeched in the terms that it is being divided, as was stated earlier, into two entities. Our amendments will try to strengthen the CBC mandate and to stop government steps which we feel are working to remove or water down the national unity concept that is part of this bill and, also, to split the CBC board into French and English units which we feel may be essentially counterproductive.
On the second front, the cable industry is really the big winner in this bill. Our amendments will hopefully present our position that the industry should be regulated as a carrier with rate of return legislation. Its ability to originate programs should also be limited, as should
Government Orders
its-at this point, anyway-almost unrestricted ability to import foreign programming.
On a third front, Mr. Speaker, are the private broadcasters. In Canada, private television has not been doing the kind of job in terms of creating truly Canadian programming that it should be doing. It has not been fulfilling that very important mandate in terms of broadcasting as a tool for nation-building. It has been falling down in that area, and I think that there needs to be safeguards in this legislation to make sure that it does fulfil that mandate.
The fourth point is with regard to the CRTC. Through this legislation, the government essentially is threatening to compromise the independence of the commission which is very vital in terms of the issues facing the broadcasting industry in Canada today. In making this point, I hope that we will also be able to present reasons to be critical of the commission, to advocate the commission as it will be structured, and to advocate specific legislative remedies that we feel will give it the correct direction.
I know my time is limited, Mr. Speaker, but in terms of the motions before us, I want to speak specifically in regard to the first group of motions.
This group of amendments basically deals with the definition section within the bill. Motion Nos. 1, 4, and 5 deal basically with a possible threat to Canada's jurisdiction over broadcasting. Motion No. 3 is identical to the one that was presented by my colleague at the committee stage. It essentially opposes the government's measures to separate the services provided by broadcasters into programming and non-programming areas.
With respect to Motion Nos. 1, 4, and 5,1 just want to read a comment made by the CRTC in a brief presented to the committee earlier. It states says that the new act may, through the definition of broadcasting, lead to a reopening of now judicially subtle federal-provincial disputes over broadcasting, stirring up old wounds and legal issues. We can see that some of the directions in which this bill takes us are clearly running us into some troubled waters.
I see my time is up, Mr. Speaker. As the debate unfolds, I will have opportunity to comment in more

Government Orders
detail on the many amendments are being presented by my colleagues, the member for Port Moody-Coquitlam, and the Liberal member for Mount Royal.

Mr. Speaker, we are at a time in our history when we almost seem to be going through a minor nervous breakdown in the country. There is so much depression out there. The economy is not working for us.
It's true.

Yes, it is true. It is pretty eerie. To spend a weekend in Toronto and then come back here is like being in two different countries.
Traditionally in this country, the Broadcasting Act has been an instrument of national unity. It has been an agent for galvanizing the will of the country. I cannot understand why the government wants to remove those words, especially at a time when we are all so fragile.
I think of situations that have happened in the country in the past when we decentralized certain activities of the national government to the province. Never once did the province take a pass on the responsibilities that we gave to them. They maintained those powers and they exercised them with all of the resources that they have.
What concerns me is when we take a broadcast bill, such as Bill C-40, and remove the words "for the promotion of national unity", we are going to have jurisdictional disputes. Suddenly we will have a situation where the Government of Canada will have a particular point of view on an issue and a particular province will have its own definition of what its priority objective is all about. In a cultural objective, whose will is going to reign supreme? Is it going to be the national will? Or will the national will be subservient to the provincial definition?
I am very nervous because there are broadcasting situations that are evolving right now where the regulator is telling broadcasters that their English-French component of music, say, will be 60 per cent English and 40 per cent francophone. After two or three months the owners of the radio station will come back to the regulator, the CRTC, and they will say: "I can't make a go of it with 60 per cent English. I need 90 per cent French and 10 per cent English." But the regulator will
say: "Well, I am sorry. We are the ones that give this definition."
The next thing we know, we are going to be in the Supreme Court where we are going to have the national regulator, the CRTC, going to court with a provincially operated jurisdiction. The CRTC's traditional role has been through the Broadcasting Act to be concerned for the national good and national unity.
Under this new formula the provincial jurisdiction, I believe, has a valid case, because we are really saying in this act that it is the provincial cultural thrust that we must become more extremely sensitized to. Once precedent is set, Mr. Speaker, in a court like this that, we will ultimately have a situation where there will be eight or ten different cultural ghettos all across the country, The CRTC will have absolutely no ability to regulate a national thread or a national will. It will have no ability to drop the hammer and say: "Look, there are things that are good in Halifax that are good in Toronto, and that are good in Vancouver." In other words, the commonness that makes us good will no longer be there and no longer can be regulated.
Because of the very special power that the Broadcasting Act has, whether it is cable, television, or radio, I think we are really putting ourselves into a very precarious situation by not putting up a very strong objection to the words "national unity" being removed from this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to rise today to speak in support of the Liberal motions, particularly those motions that relate to the question of the CBC and broadcasting remaining in the federal jurisdiction.
What we are talking about here is a question of national unity. We are talking about an instrument of national unity, a tradition of national unity, and an institution that Canadians have looked upon since its invention as an instrument of national unity.
Later in these motions there will be specific references made to withdrawing the term that calls for the CBC to be an instrument of national unity from the Broadcast Act. I consider that, and I know that millions of Canadians would agree, to be a travesty. I consider it to be a form of sale of our birth right.

I remember 15 years ago, the first time I left Halifax and moved to British Columbia in my first job after I finished university, being particularly home sick, even though the west coast is a lovely place. I can remember listening to CBC with even more of a fervour than I did at home because it reminded me on a daily basis that this was one country from coast to coast. Listening to the news, The World at Eight every morning, listening to As it Happens every night at six, hearing the same voices giving the same news items, the same stories, the same programming right across the country was a reassuring event.
Along with that, before I left the maritimes to go to the west coast, I had been in graduate school in Great Britain. I can tell you again that the Canadians would stay up until all hours to get Radio Canada International to hear our own news, to listen to hockey games, to keep our contacts with our own sense of Canadianism that Canadian broadcasting has always given us.
For my generation, the post-war baby boom generation, we began with radio and we set wave into television. Again, I remember things that reinforced my sense of Canadianism that came from the various broadcasting institutions of this country.
I remember as a small child watching a program about children in Winnipeg. That is a city that I would not visit until I was in my late twenties, but when I got there I recognized Golden Boy, and I knew how cold it was on the comer of Portage and Main in the winter.
I look at what this bill will do to this institution of Canadian unity. I am sad and I am shocked. I look at the various things that this government wants to do and I see it as part of the pattern that we have all been forced to live with since this government was unfortunately reelected in 1988. What we see is a wholesale destruction of Canadian institutions.
One of the other things I look at here is the separation of the CBC board into two standing committees; one in English, one in French. That is really Canadian apartheid. We sit here today, knowing that our whole future constitutionally as Canadians is in difficulty, to understate the case, in jeopardy, not to overstate it. Instead of ensuring the ongoing health and welfare of an institution
Government Orders
that can be a major force for Canadian unity, we are again trying to divide and compromise this nation.
We have to listen to each other in every region and every province. One of the best ways for listening to each other is through the use of our broadcast institutions and in particular, from my point of view, through the use of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
When the Caplan-Sauvageau committee recommended the removal of the term "a force for Canadian unity" from the Broadcasting Act, they made a mistake. They made a mistake so grievous in nature that we are all going to be living with its ramifications for a long time to come. One of the things they said was that they felt that the use of the CBC, or using those terms as a force for Canadian unity, would hinder programming that could reflect the multicultural aspects of Canada, a linguistic duality, and so on. Mr. Speaker, where I come from in the province of Nova Scotia, they would have hard terms for that. The best way I can put it is to say that it is a lot of codswallop.
Why should we think that being a force for Canadian unity will diminish anyone else? Why did our ancestors come here? Why did we come here, in the case of some of our members that sit in the House? Why do people want to live in Canada? Because it is a wonderful country, because it is a diverse country, because it has all these bizarre and strange regional poles and pushes, and because we spent a great deal of our time contemplating our differences as opposed to thanking God for our blessings. But, people love this country in every single province, and they love it through their national institutions. They do not need to be told that being in favour of Canadian unity and pushing for Canadian unity is going to somehow diminish them as members of their own particular cultural groups. I cannot see how anyone could possibly make a case for that at the best of times.
I remember a long time ago being at a meeting of young people in Nova Scotia and a young man from the highlands of Cape Breton was discussing with another young man, who was the son of new Canadians. He had been bom in Canada but his parents had come from western Europe. The young man of Scottish descent, in the accent that I will not attempt to reproduce, but it is a beautiful Cape Breton accent-it is very much like my colleague from Dartmouth actually-said: "If you want to know how to preserve your culture, come to us in Cape Breton and we will show you". It is very true. With regard to the Cape Breton culture, in the words of that very famous, and justly so, son of Cape Breton, Hugh

Government Orders
MacLellan, the incidence of the kilt in Cape Breton arose commensurately with the incidence of the tourist. But Scottish culture in Cape Breton is strong, and one of the reasons it is strong is the CBC policy for Gaelic programming on a weekly basis on CBC Radio in Sydney.
The CBC was a great force in creating the Department of Celtic Studies at St. Francis Xavier University, with which some people even on the other side of the House have more than a nodding acquaintance.
In closing, let me merely say that it is stuff and nonsense to suggest that being a force for Canadian unity could possibly hinder any Canadian's development, self-expression or cultural wholeness. The federal jurisdiction must be maintained if the CBC and broadcasting in Canada is to retain the moral authority that it should have and if Canada is to have a way to speak, and Canadians are to have a way to speak to each other for the rest of what could be a wonderful future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take advantage of the opportunity to speak briefly about Bill C-40.
Let me just say, in listening to the eloquent words of my colleagues, the hon. member for Mount Royal, the hon. member for Halifax, the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood, and others who have spoken about their concerns for national unity, the implications for national unity, and the implications for federal jurisdiction as a consequence of the passage of this bill as proposed, it strikes me as incredibly ironic that today we, in Parliament, have been given notice that the government will shortly put forward a motion for consideration by Parliament a federal initiative to deal with the question of constitutional renewal in Canada. [DOT]
there is in the country an exercise in Quebec that is now under way.
There is an exercise in the maritimes under way. There may be one beginning in Ontario. The western premiers are doing their thing with respect to the future of the country. Suddenly, there is an understanding that the country cannot be defined from the perspective of a particular region or province. It has to be defined in the place and from the jurisdiction where every voice and every region is represented and where true consensus can be found, the Parliament of Canada.
The Prime Minister says: "Tomorrow, I put down a motion and tomorrow I, the Prime Minister, begin the debate." How ironic that against that backdrop, that recognition that the country more than ever is Balka-nized, divided, needs national institutions, against that backdrop today before us in the House is a bill having to do with the future of broadcasting in Canada which contributes to the Balkanization of Canada that has given rise to the need to have a debate starting tomorrow.
That is why members of the opposition, my colleague the critic and member for Mount Royal, will be proposing so many important amendments to this broadcasting bill. I tell you this bill as drafted and as it sits is not acceptable to my colleague. It is not acceptable to the Liberal Party, because this bill is not a contributor to the kind of solution the Prime Minister says he wants for the deep division and wounds that have scarred the soul of Canada. It does not contribute to healing.
It contributes to further division. We make a plea to members opposite to understand this is not just a parliamentary exercise. This is not a critic undertaking her responsibility to examine a bill and to make some proposals so we can say at the end of the day: "We did our job." This is a heartfelt plea to understand the consequence and the importance of broadcasting in Canada.

We are told that tomorrow the Prime Minister will speak to the House on that subject, that there is on the part of the government a recognition that in the vacuum of leadership that has been the reality here in Ottawa vis-a-vis the Constitution and post Meech Lake, that
Fundamentally, Mr. Speaker, when you strip away the institutions, when you privatize the Petro-Canadas, the Air Canadas, the post office, when you take down the federal flag in the smallest community in the last point on the east coast of Newfoundland, the only mirror and symbol of the nation that is left is the ability through the
October 31, 1990

CBC to come into the hearts and homes of Canadians no matter where they live and to hold up the mirror no matter where they live in Canadian society. That is what the CBC is, a huge mirror.
Sometimes it tilts on the Atlantic. Sometimes it tilts on Quebec. Other days Ontario and sometimes, the west. It reflects ourselves back at us. We do not always like what we see. We do not always even agree with what we see, but it is a focus on Canada. It is a mandate that includes the concept and the responsibility to contribute to national unity.
Do you know what, Mr. Speaker? My riding is in the great northern peninsula of Newfoundland: Port au Choix, Cook's Harbour, Croque, Griguet or Harbour Deep, a place you can only reach by boat or by airplane. Only 200 souls live in Harbour Deep.
There is no Global, because there is no advertising revenue. There is no CTV-I do not blame them-because there is no advertising revenue. There is no cable television-I do not blame them-because there is no advertising revenue.
Harbour Deep is connected with its country. It is connected with Canada. There is no post office there anymore either. It is connected with Canada, because it receives the CBC. Why does it receive the CBC? Because the CBC is mandated to be there. Cynics could suggest this bill is the first step on the road to privatization of the CBC.
We hear those who do not understand Canada, who have never seen beyond the concrete and glass towers of our large and sometimes beautiful and wonderful urban centres that there is another Canada. They talk about the CBC budget of $1.3 billion. They say: "Look at CTV. Look at how much cheaper it is. Look at Global. Look at the American networks. Look at cable. What do we have the CBC for? We can put junk programming in front of our children and the families of this nation without the CBC" but, Mr. Speaker, none of them will be found in the smaller communities of this nation. None of them will turn the mirror and reflect this country back to the Canadians who live in the rural communities of this nation, in our north, in the west, in the Atlantic, in northern Ontario, and northern Quebec. None of them will be present, or have the mandate to be present, and more important-and this is most important-none of
Government Orders
the other networks will reflect those tiny communities back to Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, or Ottawa.
That is the nature of the institution that is CBC. That is the importance of it, giving the country an opportunity to understand itself, to share each other's problem and potential, to share each other's joy, each other's culture, and language, and song, and tradition, and history, and aspirations.
This bill is not a regulatory exercise, a tinker here, and a tinker there. It is not a response to a private sector whose mandate is the bottom line.
The airwaves do not belong to the shareholders of a private concern. They belong to me. They belong to 26 million Canadians no matter where they live and they are held in trust by the government, by the Minister of Communications on behalf of 26 million Canadians who own the airwaves, and the government has to exercise that trust on behalf of all Canadians with care.
I say again at a time when already in this country we increasingly reflect almost a modern-day tower of Babylon, where people are speaking in every region, each with a different message, speaking at each other but not to each other, making noise but not listening. The nature of the broadcasting regime in Canada becomes very important. What is particularly important is the nature of the CBC.
The fabric of this country is rendered, it is tom, it is held only in this day of great cynicism and as my friend from Broadview-Greenwood said, great depression, by a few threads. Some of those threads, are the CBC. We sever them at our peril.

I also want to take a brief moment to congratulate the member for Mount Royal for her efforts in improving the proposals of the government in this regard. The member for Mount Royal is quite expert on such issues and she has acquired a reputation here on Parliament Hill in terms of her knowledge of communications, the arts, and culture.
I want the House to know how important it is for us as a country to continue to have a good and viable national broadcasting system. The member for Humber-St.

October 31, 1990
Government Orders
Barbe-Baie Verte said eloquently some moments ago that in certain parts of this country it is indeed difficult to have access to programming other than what is produced by the CBC. Of course he was referring to Canadian programming.
In some communities it goes beyond that because in fact you either get that or nothing at all.
Let us use as an example my own constituency in which, of course, programming is available even without the CBC. Some areas are well equipped with cable television. In other areas, not nearly so lucky, the major Canadian networks are generally available. I am referring to the commercial types.
What is important for us to remember, I feel, is that even for those areas that are well served by the private sector in terms of providing radio or television programming, it is economical for them to purchase their programming elsewhere, rather than produce their own. There is what I would call an almost irresistible temptation not to produce anything and simply to purchase it. When I refer to purchasing it-particularly in the English language-it all comes from the same place, that is of course south of the border.

The situation is somewhat different with French programming because we have two options. Programming is either produced here in Canada-mainly, but not exclusively, in Quebec-or imported from Europe, because our U.S. giant has yet to find an efficient way to produce French programming. However, even in that case, Mr. Speaker, there is an additional dimension. U.S. programming is purchased and a so-called voice-over is added, which means that what we hear is a Translation of the English version.
What we see in French and in English, but especially in English, is programming that makes our young people experts on Detroit or Miami, while they are incapable of telling us what Winnipeg, and in some cases Montreal or any number of other Canadian cities even look like.

That contributes to the lack of knowledge that we have of each other as Canadians, that the hon. member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte was referring to in his
excellent discourse a few moments ago. The fact that we know through television cities in a different country and landscape in a different country far better than we know our own in Canada.
I had occasion not long ago to visit the constituency of Churchill in Manitoba, a place I had never been. I saw there something absolutely beautiful, something that 99 per cent of Canadians and probably even a greater percentage have never seen-possibly never will see- that beautiful tundra landscape and the land of the polar bears.
I had never seen that in television programming except for one day last year when the polar bears all went into the community of Churchill. It made The National that night. Three or four days later, most people did not remember that event. When I described my experience of having visited that community some weeks ago to my constituents, most of them did not remember that feature of roughly the same time last year on our national, publicly-owned television because, of course, it is something that only happened once, and we are not reminded of it.
Compare that to what I call the Miami Vice phenomenon, where the streets of Miami and other cities in south Florida are seen on a weekly basis on television simply because that is part of a regular program which is produced for a very vast audience in the United States and then is sold at a relatively low cost to Canadians because of the very low unit cost of producing it.
This has a dual problem for broadcasters because the program is relatively cheap to buy from elsewhere, and because it is seen on the cablevision channels on the U.S. side and transmitted here-it is available to U.S. channels anyway-it gives the broadcasters two reasons to show them to us on our Canadian television stations and networks.
The point I am making is that there is a tremendous need for us as Canadians to realize how precious our institutions are and how important it is for us to cherish them and to try to improve them. From time to time members of this House are critical of the CBC. They will say that their leader or themselves or someone else did not get favourable coverage, the CBC costs a lot to maintain anyway and so on, therefore why do we have it. It goes beyond whether or not on a particular day one of us got good or bad television coverage on the news. It
October 31, 1990

goes more to the proposition that we need that institution for our national unity.
We need the CBC and public broadcasting generally, that includes TV Ontario and others as well. We need them as an instrument of national unity. We need them at a time, that again was described by my colleague, when we see the flag of Canada on the post office being removed. We need that at a time when other instruments of national unity are being destroyed or privatized or altered by the government.
I say this to the government across the way, but I say it to all of us as parliamentarians, that we must do our utmost to cherish those institutions that have kept us together. These institutions are even more important in an age of advancing telecommunications, institutions that can contribute to keeping us together and united in the future.

I realize I may have taken up more than my intended two or three minutes, Mr. Speaker, but I did not intend to speak to all the motions. I simply wanted to inform the parliamentary secretary and other members that I consider these instruments to be very important and that I wish everybody would realize that we have the tools to help build our national unity. Safeguard it, improve it, but let's not do anything to diminish or destroy it.
